title: The Best Ways to Use One-Pagers
author: Andrew Watson
summary: Andrew Watson argues that 'one-pager' research summaries -- increasingly popular handy graphics-and-headings distillations of cognitive science topics -- mostly fail to build the understanding they promise, precisely because they invite a passive, quick-read use pattern. He identifies three strategies that actually work: making your own one-pager, since learning happens through the generative work of researching and organizing, not through the finished artifact; actively editing or arguing with someone else's one-pager, which requires enough existing expertise to meaningfully engage; and using a single one-pager intensively over days, as with Sherrington and Caviglioli's Walkthrus, dwelling on each step rather than skimming the whole. He warns that all three effective strategies require either genuine expertise or genuine sustained time, meaning the single most common use case -- a quick read by a relative novice -- is also the least effective one.
points: Watson's central claim: the person who learns the most from a one-pager is the person who makes it, because creating one requires the generative learning activities that actually build durable understanding.

He identifies a 'one-pager paradox': one-pagers genuinely benefit their creators, genuinely benefit experts who can actively argue with or edit them, and genuinely benefit novices who dwell on one intensively over days, but not beginners using them for a quick read.
His Walkthrus example shows the intensive-use strategy in practice: spending a day or two per step of a five-step guide, rather than reading the whole one-pager once and moving on.
He frames the common quick-read use pattern as actively counterproductive, creating 'the illusion of understanding' that discourages the deeper study actually required to learn a topic.
quotes: The person who learns the most from a one-pager is the person who makes the one pager.
In other words, you need to do all those generative learning activities that are most likely to ensure that you learn and remember new ideas.
Notice the key here: focused work over time. We don't get the benefit of walkthrus by reading Walkthrus. We get the benefit by choosing one of them and dwelling on it for meaningful periods of time.
This process creates the illusion of understanding; I believe that I have learned something about worked examples.

They DO benefit the people who create them... They DO benefit people who already know a great deal about a topic... But they DON'T benefit beginners who use them as their form invites us to use them: a quick read.
